title: Kava and Alcohol: Is It Safe to Mix? Sedation and Liver Risks
excerpt: Can you mix kava and alcohol? Why the two add up to more sedation, what the kava liver research really shows, how long to wait, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you mix kava and alcohol? Why they add up to more sedation, what the kava liver research shows, how long to wait between them, and warning signs.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to mix kava and alcohol. Both are depressants that slow your brain down, and taken together they appear to add to each other, so you end up more sedated, more uncoordinated, and more impaired than you'd expect from either one alone. Both also put work on your liver, and the rare but serious cases of kava-linked liver injury have often involved people who were also drinking or taking other medicines. A shell of traditional kava on its own is generally low risk for a healthy adult. A shell of kava followed by three beers is a different story.

**The quick rules:** Don't drink alcohol in the same session you drink kava, and don't take kava capsules or extracts to "come down" after a night out. If you've had kava, wait until the next day before drinking, and if you've been drinking, wait until you're fully sober before using kava. Never drive after either. If you have liver disease, drink heavily on a regular basis, or take prescription medicines (especially anything for anxiety, sleep, pain, or seizures), talk to your doctor or pharmacist before using kava at all.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and safety guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor before using kava if** you have liver disease or have been told your liver enzymes are high, you drink alcohol most days, you're pregnant or breastfeeding, or you take any medicine that causes drowsiness or is processed by the liver. **Get medical help right away if** someone who mixed kava and alcohol is hard to wake, breathing slowly, vomiting while drowsy, or confused, or if you notice yellow skin or eyes, dark urine, or pain under your right ribs after using kava. In an emergency, call 911.

## What Kava Actually Is

Kava (also called kava kava, or by its scientific name *Piper methysticum*) is a plant in the pepper family grown across the Pacific Islands, including Fiji, Vanuatu, Tonga, Samoa, and Hawaii. For centuries people there have ground the root and mixed it with water to make a muddy, earthy drink served at ceremonies and social gatherings. It's a big part of community life in those cultures, roughly the way a pint at the local pub is in others.

The active compounds are called **kavalactones**. There are several of them, with names like kavain, dihydrokavain, and methysticin. They produce a calm, relaxed feeling, a numb or tingly mouth, and, at higher amounts, heavy limbs and sleepiness. Unlike alcohol, kava doesn't usually make people loud or disinhibited. Regular kava drinkers often describe a "clear-headed" relaxation, though that clarity fades as the amount goes up.

Today kava comes in a few different forms, and the difference matters for safety:

- **Traditional water-based drinks.** Ground root mixed with water, as served in the Pacific and in most kava bars. This is the form with the longest track record.
- **Powders and "instant" kava.** Dried root or dried extract you mix into water yourself.
- **Capsules, tablets, tinctures, and concentrated extracts.** These are often made using alcohol or other solvents to pull out kavalactones, and they can deliver a much stronger, more concentrated dose. Many of the liver injury reports involved this kind of product.
- **Kava shots and "relaxation drinks."** Ready-to-drink canned or bottled products, usually with flavorings and sometimes other calming herbs.

In the US, kava is sold as a dietary supplement. That means it isn't reviewed for safety or effectiveness before it hits the shelves, and the amount of kavalactones, the part of the plant used, and the quality can vary a lot from product to product.

## Why Kava and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Brain Side

Alcohol makes you feel relaxed and sleepy mainly by boosting the activity of **GABA**, your brain's main "slow down" chemical messenger. It does this by acting on GABA-A receptors, the same family of receptors that drugs like Xanax and Valium work on.

Kavalactones appear to act on GABA-A receptors too, though in a somewhat different way, and they also affect several other targets in the brain and nerves, including some that control how easily nerve cells fire. The details are still being worked out by researchers. The practical point is simpler: **kava and alcohol both turn down your brain's activity, and they seem to do it through overlapping pathways.** Stack them and the effects add up.

What that looks like in real life:

- **More sedation.** You get drowsier faster, and you may fall asleep somewhere you didn't plan to.
- **Worse coordination and reaction time.** Walking, balance, and driving skills drop further than they would with the same amount of alcohol alone.
- **Harder to judge how impaired you are.** Kava's calm, "I feel fine" quality can mask how much the alcohol is affecting you, and the alcohol can make it harder to notice how strong the kava is.
- **More nausea and vomiting risk.** Both can upset your stomach, and vomiting while very drowsy is dangerous because of the risk of choking.

### What the research shows

There isn't a large body of research on this exact combination, but what exists points the same way. Animal studies going back decades found that kava extracts made the sedating effects of alcohol stronger and longer. A small human study published in the late 1990s tested kava, alcohol, and the two together on attention and coordination tasks, and found that the combination caused more impairment than either one alone, with volunteers also rating themselves as more intoxicated.

Small studies have limits, and some other research has found smaller effects. But "probably makes you more impaired than you realize" is a reasonable conclusion, and it matches what pharmacists and drug interaction references advise: avoid combining them.

## Why Kava and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Liver Side

This is the part that gets the most attention, and for good reason.

### The kava liver scare

In the late 1990s and early 2000s, doctors in Europe reported a series of cases of serious liver injury in people taking kava supplements. A few of these cases led to liver transplants or death. In response, Germany and several other European countries restricted or banned kava products in the early 2000s, and in 2002 the US Food and Drug Administration issued a consumer advisory warning about the potential for severe liver injury from kava-containing supplements.

Later reviews, including work by the World Health Organization, looked more closely at those cases. Several patterns came up again and again:

- **Many cases involved concentrated extracts** made with alcohol or acetone, not traditional water-based drinks.
- **Product quality was a likely factor.** Some products may have used parts of the plant other than the root, such as stems and peelings, or lower-quality kava varieties.
- **Many people were also drinking alcohol or taking other medicines** that are hard on the liver.
- **Some cases were hard to attribute** to kava alone because of other health issues or missing information.

A German court later overturned that country's ban, and the debate has settled into something like this: liver injury from kava appears to be rare, it seems to be linked more to certain products and to combinations with other substances, and traditional water-based kava from good-quality root seems to carry a lower risk. "Rare" is not "never," though, and nobody can tell you in advance whether your liver will be the unlucky one.

### Why alcohol makes the liver risk worse

Your liver breaks down both kava and alcohol. Lab studies suggest kavalactones can slow down several of the liver enzymes (from the cytochrome P450 family) that process drugs and toxins, including one called CYP2E1 that also handles alcohol. That raises the possibility of each one changing how the other is cleared, and of other medicines building up in your body.

Alcohol also adds its own stress. Heavy drinking inflames the liver, causes fat to build up in liver cells, and depletes the liver's antioxidant defenses. Adding a substance with a known, if rare, liver injury signal on top of that load is not a smart bet, especially if you drink often.

Heavy, long-term kava use is also linked to raised liver enzymes on blood tests. In studies of regular kava drinkers, these raised levels have generally come back down after people stopped. Heavy alcohol use raises some of the same markers. If you use both regularly and get a blood test, your doctor needs to know about both.

## Can You Drink Alcohol After Kava?

It's best to wait until the next day. Kava's noticeable effects usually start within 20 to 30 minutes and fade over a few hours, but how long it lasts depends on how much you had, what form it was in, and your own body. The compounds also stay in your system for a while after the obvious effects wear off.

Some practical guidance:

- **Don't go from the kava bar to a regular bar.** This is the most common real-world way people end up combining the two.
- **Don't drink alcohol the same evening you've had kava**, even if you feel sober. Kava's relaxed feeling can fool you into thinking you're fine.
- **If you had a small amount of kava early in the day**, that's less concerning than a heavy session right before going out, but there's still no benefit to cutting it close.
- **Never drive.** Kava on its own can impair driving, and people have been arrested and charged with impaired driving after heavy kava use. Combined with alcohol, the risk is higher.

## Can You Take Kava After Drinking? (Kava for a Hangover)

Some people reach for kava after a night out, either to help them fall asleep while still buzzed or to calm the shaky, anxious feeling the next morning (sometimes called "hangxiety"). Neither is a good idea.

**Taking kava while you're still drunk** stacks two depressants at the worst possible time, when alcohol is still in your blood and your judgment is already off. It can deepen sedation, and it adds to the work your liver is already doing.

**Taking kava the morning after** is less risky if the alcohol has fully cleared, but there's no good evidence that kava helps with a hangover. It doesn't rehydrate you, it doesn't settle your stomach, and it doesn't speed up how your body deals with the leftovers of alcohol. It may take the edge off anxiety for a few hours, but so might rest, food, water, and time, without the liver question. If morning-after anxiety is a regular thing for you, our guide to [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) explains why it happens and what actually helps.

If you're wired and can't sleep after drinking, don't add a sedative. Our article on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) covers safer ways to handle a restless night.

## Is Kava Safer Than Alcohol?

This is a fair question, and it's why kava bars have been popping up across the US as an alcohol-free night out. Here's an honest comparison.

| | Kava (traditional, water-based) | Alcohol |
|---|---|---|
| Main effect | Calm, relaxed, sometimes sleepy | Relaxed, disinhibited, sleepy at higher amounts |
| Hangover | Usually mild; some people feel groggy or "heavy" the next morning | Common and often significant |
| Liver | Rare reports of serious injury, mostly tied to extracts and combinations; heavy use can raise liver enzymes | Well-established cause of fatty liver, hepatitis, and cirrhosis with heavy use |
| Dependence | Not generally considered addictive in the way alcohol is | Can cause physical dependence and dangerous withdrawal |
| Driving | Can impair driving, especially in large amounts | Impairs driving even at moderate amounts |
| Regulation in the US | Sold as a supplement, quality varies | Regulated as a beverage, strength is labeled |

For a healthy adult, a moderate amount of traditional kava is likely a gentler choice than a night of heavy drinking. But "safer than alcohol" doesn't mean safe in any amount, and it definitely doesn't mean safe *with* alcohol. The comparison only works if you're choosing one instead of the other.

### A note on kava bars and kratom

Many kava bars also sell **kratom**, a different plant from Southeast Asia with opioid-like effects at higher doses. Kratom is not kava, and it carries its own risks, including dependence and dangerous interactions with alcohol and other sedatives. The FDA has warned consumers against using kratom. If you go to a kava bar, know exactly what's in your cup, and don't mix either one with alcohol.

## Does Kava Help With Alcohol Cravings or Cutting Back?

You'll see claims online that kava can help people drink less, ease cravings, or get through withdrawal. There is no good evidence that kava treats alcohol cravings or alcohol withdrawal. A few researchers have been interested in the idea because of kava's calming effects, but it hasn't been shown to work in proper human trials.

Some people do find that swapping a weeknight beer for a cup of kava or another non-alcoholic option helps them cut back. That's a personal choice, and for some it works. But two cautions:

- **Don't use kava to self-treat withdrawal.** If you've been drinking heavily and notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, anxiety, or trouble sleeping when you stop, those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can become dangerous. Talk to a doctor. There are safe, effective medical options, and you shouldn't try to handle it with a supplement.
- **Swapping one daily habit for another isn't automatically healthier.** Heavy daily kava use has its own effects, including dry, scaly skin and raised liver enzymes.

## What About Kava Supplements and Anxiety?

Many people use kava capsules for anxiety rather than as a social drink. The evidence here is mixed. A 2013 randomized trial by Jerome Sarris and colleagues found that a water-based kava extract reduced anxiety in people with generalized anxiety disorder over six weeks compared with placebo. A larger 16-week trial by the same research group, published in 2020, did not find a meaningful difference between kava and placebo, and more people in the kava group showed raised liver enzymes.

So kava may help some people with anxiety, but it's not a sure thing, and it's not a casual supplement to pair with drinking. If you're using kava daily for anxiety, that's a strong reason to keep alcohol light or avoid it altogether, and to tell your doctor so they can check your liver if needed. For a broader comparison of calming supplements, see our [GABA guide](/never-hungover/gaba-gamma-aminobutyric-acid-complete-guide-benefits-dosage-natural-sources-2025) and our article on [ashwagandha and alcohol](/never-hungover/ashwagandha-and-alcohol).

## Kava, Alcohol, and Medications

Because kava seems to affect both brain activity and liver enzymes, it can interact with a lot of medicines. Adding alcohol to the mix makes those interactions harder to predict. Be especially careful, and ask a pharmacist first, if you take:

- **Benzodiazepines** such as Xanax (alprazolam), Valium (diazepam), or Ativan (lorazepam). These already carry a serious warning about alcohol; adding kava piles on more sedation. Our guide to [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) explains why that combination is so dangerous.
- **Sleep medicines** such as Ambien (zolpidem) or sedating antihistamines like Benadryl.
- **Opioid painkillers**, including codeine, hydrocodone, and oxycodone.
- **Seizure and nerve-pain medicines**, such as gabapentin and pregabalin. See our [gabapentin and alcohol](/never-hungover/gabapentin-and-alcohol) article for more on how those interact with drinking.
- **Antidepressants and antipsychotics**, some of which are sedating or processed by the same liver enzymes.
- **Parkinson's medicines** such as levodopa. There are reports of kava making Parkinson's symptoms worse.
- **Acetaminophen (Tylenol) and other medicines that can strain the liver.**

This list isn't complete. If you take any prescription medicine regularly, the safest step is a quick check with your pharmacist before adding kava.

## Who Should Avoid Kava (With or Without Alcohol)

Skip kava entirely, or only use it with your doctor's okay, if you:

- Have **liver disease**, hepatitis, fatty liver, or raised liver enzymes
- **Drink alcohol most days** or binge regularly
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**
- Take **sedating medicines** or medicines processed heavily by the liver
- Have **Parkinson's disease** or depression that's being treated
- Are having **surgery** soon (sedation and anesthesia interactions)
- Are under 18

## Kava Hangover vs Alcohol Hangover

Kava can leave some people feeling foggy, heavy, or slow the next morning, especially after a large session. People sometimes call this a "kava hangover." It's usually milder than an alcohol hangover and tends to lack the headache, nausea, and dehydration that alcohol brings, because kava doesn't act as a diuretic the way alcohol does and doesn't produce the same toxic by-products.

If you combine the two, though, you don't get the gentler kava version. You get an alcohol hangover, possibly worse because of poorer sleep quality and extra work for your liver, plus kava grogginess on top. Mixing them is a reliable way to feel worse the next day.

## Warning Signs: When to Get Help

**Get emergency help (call 911) if someone who mixed kava and alcohol:**

- Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting off mid-sentence
- Is breathing slowly or irregularly
- Is vomiting while very drowsy or passed out
- Is confused, has bluish lips or skin, or has a seizure

Don't leave them alone to "sleep it off." Lay them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them until help arrives.

**See a doctor soon if, after using kava, you notice:**

- Yellowing of your skin or the whites of your eyes
- Dark urine or pale stools
- Pain or tenderness under the right side of your ribs
- Unusual tiredness, loss of appetite, or nausea that doesn't go away

These can be signs of liver trouble. Stop using kava and tell your doctor about any kava, alcohol, and medicines you've been taking.

## A Better Plan for Your Night Out

If you're looking up "kava and alcohol" because you want to relax and feel good the next day, the best approach is to pick one, not both:

- **Choosing kava?** Go with a traditional water-based drink from a reputable source, keep the amount modest, skip alcohol that day, and don't drive.
- **Choosing alcohol?** Eat a real meal first, pace yourself, alternate drinks with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people who drink also take a liver-support supplement. Here's an honest look:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research comes from animal and lab studies, with a small amount of human data, including a 2015 randomized trial in people with fatty liver disease that found improvements in some liver markers. It's promising, but there is no good evidence that DHM makes it safe to combine kava and alcohol, and you shouldn't treat it as a way around the advice above. Because DHM may also act on the brain's GABA system, don't add it to a day you've had kava. Our [supplement reviews](/reviews) cover the options for ordinary drinking nights, and our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when.
- **Milk thistle** is the most-studied liver herb, with mixed human evidence but a good safety record. See our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements) for how the options compare.

No supplement cancels out the risk of stacking two sedatives, so the rule doesn't change: kava or alcohol, not both.

## The Bottom Line

- Kava and alcohol both slow your brain down, and together they appear to make you more impaired than either one alone.
- Both are processed by the liver. Serious liver injury from kava is rare, but alcohol use, concentrated extracts, and other medicines have shown up often in the reported cases.
- Don't drink alcohol the same day you've had kava, and don't use kava to calm down or sleep after drinking.
- Traditional water-based kava is probably a gentler night out than heavy drinking, but only as a replacement, never as a mixer.
- If you have liver problems, drink most days, or take sedating or prescription medicines, talk to your doctor before using kava.
- Anyone very drowsy, hard to wake, or breathing slowly after mixing the two needs emergency help.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you mix kava and alcohol?**

It's best not to. Kava and alcohol are both depressants that seem to act on overlapping brain pathways, so together they can cause more sedation and impairment than either alone. Both are also processed by the liver, and many reported cases of kava-related liver injury involved people who were also drinking. Choose one or the other, not both.

**How long after kava can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting time, but a sensible rule is to wait until the next day. Kava's noticeable effects usually fade within a few hours, but how long they last depends on the amount and form you took, and the compounds stay in your body longer than the feeling does. Don't go straight from a kava bar to drinking, even if you feel sober.

**Can I take kava after drinking to relax or sleep?**

No. Taking kava while alcohol is still in your system stacks two sedatives and adds to your liver's workload. There's also no good evidence that kava helps with a hangover. If you can't sleep after drinking, rest, water, and time are safer than adding another depressant.

**Is kava bad for your liver if you also drink?**

Liver injury from kava is rare, but it has been reported, and many of those cases involved concentrated extracts, poor-quality products, alcohol, or other medicines. Heavy drinking already strains the liver, so combining regular alcohol use with kava raises the stakes. If you drink most days or have any liver condition, talk to your doctor before using kava.

**Is kava a safe alternative to alcohol?**

For a healthy adult, a moderate amount of traditional water-based kava is likely gentler than a night of heavy drinking, with a milder next-day effect and a lower risk of dependence. It still causes impairment, can affect driving, and has rare liver risks. It works as a replacement for alcohol, not as something to mix with it.

**Does kava help with alcohol cravings or withdrawal?**

There is no good evidence that kava treats alcohol cravings or withdrawal. If you notice shaking, sweating, a racing heart, or anxiety when you stop drinking, talk to a doctor, because alcohol withdrawal can become dangerous and there are effective medical treatments for it.

**What's the difference between a kava hangover and an alcohol hangover?**

A kava hangover is usually mild grogginess or heaviness the next morning, without the headache, nausea, and dehydration that alcohol often causes. Mixing kava with alcohol doesn't give you the milder version; you get an alcohol hangover plus kava grogginess on top.

**Does DHM make it safe to mix kava and alcohol?**

No. There is no good evidence that DHM protects against the combined sedation or liver effects of kava and alcohol. DHM has promising early research on alcohol metabolism and liver health, mostly from animal studies, but it doesn't change the advice to avoid mixing the two.
